parts.label: (a)
key_concepts: spontaneous de-excitation and re-emission in all directions
hints: Hint 1: Think about what the cool gas contains and what the incident light is made of at the particle level.
Hint 2: Consider when an electron in a low energy level can take energy from the beam - what condition on the photon must be met?
Hint 3: Think about what happens very soon after an electron has been raised to a higher level - can it stay there?
Hint 4: Compare the direction of the original beam with the directions in which the gas gives out light again - what does this mean for light seen straight through?
parts.proper_answer: Photons interact with electrons in the gas atoms. A photon is absorbed only if its energy $hf$ exactly equals the difference between two electron energy levels, exciting an electron to a higher level. The excited electron soon de-excites, re-emitting a photon of the same energy in a random direction. That wavelength is therefore removed from the forward beam, giving a dark line in the continuous spectrum.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture the cool gas**
You have white-like light with every wavelength from 420 nm to 740 nm hitting atoms that are mostly in their low energy states. Think of light as a stream of photons, each with energy $E = hf$. Think of the atom as having electrons that can only sit on fixed energy steps.

Step 2: **Absorption is selective**
An electron can only absorb a photon if the photon gives it exactly the energy needed to jump up: $$hf = E_{high} - E_{low}$$ If the photon is too big or too small it just passes by. So only certain wavelengths are taken out of the beam, each one lifting an electron to a higher level.

Step 3: **Re-emission does not go forward**
The excited state is unstable. Very quickly the electron falls back down and gives out a photon of the same energy. But this re-emitted photon can go out in any random direction, not just along the original beam.

Step 4: **Why you see dark lines**
Looking straight through along the incident direction you see the full continuous spectrum minus those absorbed wavelengths. Very little of the re-emitted light comes to your eye in that direction, so at each absorbed wavelength there is a dark absorption line.

parts.label: (b)(i)
key_concepts: photon energy inversely proportional to wavelength
hints: Hint 1: Recall how the energy carried by a photon changes when its wavelength gets longer - longer $\lambda$ means smaller frequency $f$.
Hint 2: Use the given 420 nm value to scale to 740 nm, or calculate directly from $E = hc/\lambda$ and then convert joules to eV.
parts.proper_answer: $E = 1.68\text{ eV}$ (photons in beam have energies $1.68\text{ eV}$ to $2.96\text{ eV}$).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use inverse proportionality**
For photons, $$E = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$$ so $E$ is proportional to $1/\lambda$. That means you can scale from the known value without needing $h$ and $c$: $$E_{740} = E_{420} \times \frac{\lambda_{420}}{\lambda_{740}}$$

Step 2: **Put numbers in**
$$E_{740} = 2.96 \times \frac{420}{740} \approx 1.68\text{ eV}$$ The same result follows from $$E = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.0 \times 10^{8}}{740 \times 10^{-9}} = 2.69 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J} = 1.68\text{ eV}$$ since $1\text{ eV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$. So the incident beam provides photon energies from about $1.68\text{ eV}$ up to $2.96\text{ eV}$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
key_concepts: matching photon energy to level difference
transitions from n=2 level at -3.4 eV
hints: Hint 1: List the possible upward jumps and work out their energy differences - only those between about 1.68 eV and 2.96 eV can be caused by this beam.
Hint 2: Remember the gas is cool, so almost all electrons start from the lowest of the levels shown that can be reached by visible photons - think about which lower level to draw all arrows from.
parts.proper_answer: Dark lines are due to absorption from the $-3.4\text{ eV}$ level: $-3.4\text{ eV} \rightarrow -1.5\text{ eV}$ ($1.9\text{ eV}$), $-3.4\text{ eV} \rightarrow -0.85\text{ eV}$ ($2.55\text{ eV}$), $-3.4\text{ eV} \rightarrow -0.54\text{ eV}$ ($2.86\text{ eV}$). All lie in the $1.68$ to $2.96\text{ eV}$ range.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Start from the populated level**
In a cool gas electrons are in low states. The ground state at $-13.6\text{ eV}$ needs about $10\text{ eV}$ to excite, far above the $1.68$ to $2.96\text{ eV}$ available. The next level up at $-3.4\text{ eV}$ is the effective lower level for visible absorption.

Step 2: **Find matching jumps**
Calculate differences from $-3.4\text{ eV}$: $$-3.4 \rightarrow -1.5 : 1.9\text{ eV}$$ $$-3.4 \rightarrow -0.85 : 2.55\text{ eV}$$ $$-3.4 \rightarrow -0.54 : 2.86\text{ eV}$$ All three are between $1.68\text{ eV}$ and $2.96\text{ eV}$, so photons of those energies in the beam are absorbed. Draw three upward arrows on Fig. 11.2 starting at $-3.4\text{ eV}$ and ending at $-1.5\text{ eV}$, $-0.85\text{ eV}$ and $-0.54\text{ eV}$.
